topic: Setting up two-step sign-in and a password manager at work
scope_note: Practical, generic guidance for employees on two-step sign-in with an authenticator app, a password manager, backup codes and a lost phone. No brand names, no breach statistics. Company IT policy overrides anything generic here.

facts.statement: Credential stuffing is when attackers take a username and password leaked from one site and try the same pair on many other sites.
facts.reference_hint: OWASP, Credential Stuffing description; NCSC (UK) password guidance

facts.statement: Reusing one password across sites means a leak at one site can open every other account that uses the same password, including a work account.
facts.reference_hint: NCSC (UK) password guidance; NIST SP 800-63B

facts.statement: Phishing tricks a person into typing their password into a fake sign-in page, so even a strong password can be handed over.
facts.reference_hint: CISA phishing guidance

facts.statement: Passwords from past breaches circulate in lists that attackers try against other accounts, so a password that has appeared in a leak is unsafe to keep using.
facts.reference_hint: NIST SP 800-63B, which advises checking chosen passwords against lists of compromised passwords

facts.statement: Two-step sign-in (two-factor or multi-factor authentication) asks for a second proof besides the password: something you know, the password, plus something you have, such as your phone.
facts.reference_hint: NIST SP 800-63B, authentication factors; CISA multifactor authentication guidance

facts.statement: With two-step sign-in on, a stolen or leaked password alone is no longer enough to get into the account, because the attacker also needs the second factor.
facts.reference_hint: CISA multifactor authentication guidance

facts.statement: Two-step sign-in does not make an account unhackable: it removes the easy route, but a user can still be tricked into approving or typing a code on a fake page.
facts.caveat: Say it calmly: it raises the bar a lot, it is not a guarantee.
facts.reference_hint: CISA, phishing-resistant MFA fact sheets

facts.statement: An authenticator app generates a short one-time code on your phone from a secret key that is shared once, when you scan the QR code at setup.
facts.reference_hint: RFC 6238 (TOTP)

facts.statement: Typical setup steps are: open the account's security settings, turn on two-step sign-in, choose authenticator app, scan the QR code with the app, then type the current 6-digit code to confirm.
facts.caveat: Menu names and order differ between services; the narrator should say 'typically' and use generic labels.
facts.reference_hint: Common pattern across services; RFC 6238 for the codes

facts.statement: The authenticator code is time-based and changes about every 30 seconds, so you type the code currently on screen.
facts.caveat: 30 seconds is the usual interval recommended by the standard; some services use another interval.
facts.reference_hint: RFC 6238 (TOTP), default time step

facts.statement: At setup the service usually shows backup or recovery codes, and these are often displayed only once.
facts.caveat: Behaviour varies by service; some let you generate a new set later. Say 'usually'.
facts.reference_hint: Common service behaviour; CISA account recovery guidance

facts.statement: Each backup code can typically be used once, as a stand-in for the app code when you cannot reach your authenticator.
facts.reference_hint: Common service behaviour

facts.statement: Backup codes should be stored somewhere safe and separate from the phone alone, for example in the password manager or printed and kept securely, following your company's policy.
facts.caveat: Where to store them is a company policy question; point viewers to IT. Do not store them only on the phone that might be lost.
facts.reference_hint: NIST SP 800-63B recovery guidance; CISA

facts.statement: A password manager stores your logins in an encrypted vault that you unlock with one master password.
facts.reference_hint: NCSC (UK) password manager guidance

facts.statement: The master password should be a long passphrase that is easy for you to remember but hard for others to guess, since it protects everything in the vault.
facts.reference_hint: NCSC (UK) three random words advice; NIST SP 800-63B favours length over complexity rules

facts.statement: Password managers can generate long random passwords, so each account can have its own unique password that you never need to remember or type.
facts.reference_hint: NCSC (UK) password manager guidance; NIST SP 800-63B

facts.statement: You can save an existing login in a password manager by signing in once and accepting the manager's offer to save it, or by adding it by hand, and then replace weak or reused passwords with generated ones.
facts.caveat: Exact prompts vary by tool; describe generically.
facts.reference_hint: Common password manager behaviour

facts.statement: Autofill in a password manager normally fills a login only on the site address saved with it, so it may not fill on a look-alike fake page, which is a warning sign.
facts.caveat: A helpful signal, not a guarantee; browser extensions and settings differ, so do not tell viewers to rely on it alone.
facts.reference_hint: NCSC (UK) password manager guidance; NIST SP 800-63B discussion of autofill and paste

facts.statement: The password manager vendor usually cannot recover a forgotten master password, so it must be one you will remember, and the company may offer its own recovery route.
facts.caveat: Typical for consumer-style designs; business tools may have admin recovery. Point to IT.
facts.reference_hint: Common zero-knowledge design; vendor documentation varies

facts.statement: Codes sent by text message (SMS) are considered weaker than codes from an authenticator app, because messages can be intercepted or redirected, for example by SIM swapping.
facts.caveat: SMS is still better than a password alone. Say 'weaker', not 'useless'.
facts.reference_hint: NIST SP 800-63B treats SMS out-of-band as a restricted authenticator; CISA MFA guidance

facts.statement: Current NIST guidance favours long passwords and passphrases over forced complexity rules, and advises against forcing regular password changes unless there is evidence of compromise.
facts.reference_hint: NIST SP 800-63B, memorized secrets

facts.statement: If your phone is lost, sign in with a backup code, report the loss to IT or the helpdesk promptly, set up the authenticator again on the new phone, then remove the old device and sign out other sessions.
facts.caveat: Exact steps and wording vary by service and company; IT's instructions come first.
facts.reference_hint: CISA and NCSC (UK) lost-device guidance; typical service behaviour

facts.statement: Reporting a lost phone quickly lets IT revoke access and check the account, and it limits the time someone else could use the device.
facts.reference_hint: NCSC (UK) guidance on lost or stolen devices

terms.meaning: signing in with your password plus a second proof, such as a code from your phone; also called two-factor or multi-factor authentication
a phone app that shows a short code that changes about every 30 seconds
a one-time code shown at setup that lets you sign in when you cannot use your authenticator app
the one long passphrase that unlocks your password manager
trying a leaked username and password on many other sites

not_claimed: Two-step sign-in makes an account unhackable.
Changing passwords every 30 days is best practice.
Passwords need symbols, capitals and numbers to be strong: length matters more than forced complexity.
Any breach statistic or percentage of attacks stopped by two-step sign-in.
SMS codes are as strong as an authenticator app.
Password managers cannot be hacked or are risk-free.
Specific product or brand names or their menu labels.
A specific company policy on backup code storage or approved apps: that is IT's call.
